title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 33–34
description: Curated B2 terminology, technical verbs and word-use patterns for science, technology and computers, with original English examples and Brazilian Portuguese glosses.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary selection follows the study pages, illustrated labels, exercises and relevant answer key. Teaching notes and example sentences are independently written; book passages, exercise texts and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Scientific field definitions, technology illustrations, technical collocations, computer terminology and processes, full exercise pages and corresponding printed answer-key entries reviewed.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British English IPA supplied for high-confidence words and short phrases. Longer or uncertain transcriptions are left empty rather than guessed; connected-speech and regional variants are not exhaustively marked.
audit.languagePolicy: All fields are in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Comparison of the uploaded study and exercise pages with illustrations and the printed answer key; independently authored teaching examples and notes; automated offline JSON structure, IDs, provenance and audio-target checks. No live import, browser TTS or speech-recognition testing performed.
audit.limitations: No audio recordings are bundled. No live VocabLab app or speech testing was done. Technology examples reflect textbook vocabulary and some devices, such as 3D TVs and DVD drives, may be less common today.

units.title: Unit 33 — Science and technology
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 33. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Name newer scientific fields and explain their focus, including genetics, ergonomics, molecular biology and hydroponics.
Identify everyday digital devices and explain their functions.
Use scientific and technical verbs with appropriate objects and prepositions, distinguishing formal alternatives from everyday verbs.
Apply the source exercises’ scientific collocations and hereditary-feature vocabulary accurately.

sectionsChecked: A: New science branches, table definitions and accompanying numbered glosses
B: Illustrated smartphone, tablet, 3D TV, camcorder, satnav/GPS and digital photo-frame labels
C: Scientific verbs, equipment and collocations; formal technical alternatives
Exercises 33.1–33.4 and printed answer key, including hereditary-feature terminology and scientific verbs

items.example: Genetic engineering is used to investigate how specific genes affect crops.
items.note: The field involves changing genetic material in living organisms.

items.example: The researchers collected a DNA sample for analysis.
items.note: Short for deoxyribonucleic acid; the molecule that carries genetic information.

items.example: Some shoppers look for labels on genetically modified foods.
items.note: The abbreviation GM stands for genetically modified; the wider meaning includes genetic changes, not only transgenic ones.

items.example: Changing this parameter could alter the response of the system.
items.note: To make something different, often slightly; the object follows alter directly.

items.example: Researchers studied which features of the plants were inherited.
items.note: A significant quality or characteristic; in technology also a function.

items.example: Good ergonomics can make a workstation more comfortable.
items.note: Studies how tools and physical workspaces fit their users.

items.example: The team redesigned the working environment to reduce discomfort.
items.note: Here it means the physical setting in which people work.

items.example: The experiment examines how operators interact with the interface.
items.note: Use the preposition with for interaction between people, devices or systems.

items.example: She specialises in molecular biology and cell processes.
items.note: The study of molecules and processes involved in living organisms.

items.example: The team examined the structure of the protein.
items.note: Refers to how parts are arranged or organised.

items.example: Scientists are still investigating the function of this molecule.
items.note: In science, function means what something does, not how it is built.

items.example: A water molecule contains oxygen and hydrogen atoms.
items.note: A group of atoms bonded together.

items.example: This condition is associated with several environmental factors.
items.note: Associated with is a common scientific link between related phenomena.

items.example: Voice technology can make equipment easier to control without a keyboard.
items.note: Technology that recognises, processes or produces human speech.

items.example: The system must interpret speech reliably in a noisy room.
items.note: Interpret means establish the intended meaning or content.

items.example: The sensor enables the machine to detect small movements.
items.note: Pattern: enable somebody or something to do something.

items.pt: software de transcrição de voz em texto
items.example: Voice-to-text software creates a transcript from a recording.
items.note: Converts spoken words into written text.

items.example: Stem cell research explores possible ways to repair damaged tissue.
items.note: Research into cells able to develop into different types of specialised cells.

items.example: The microscope image showed several healthy cells.
items.note: The smallest structural unit of a living organism.

items.example: Cloning raises scientific and ethical questions in agriculture.
items.note: Producing genetically identical copies of a cell or organism.

items.example: A change in one gene may affect several characteristics.
items.note: A unit of hereditary information contained in DNA.

items.example: The creation of a digital model took several months.
items.note: Noun from create, meaning the act of making something.

items.example: The greenhouse uses hydroponics to grow lettuce without soil.
items.note: A method of growing plants in nutrient-containing water rather than soil.

items.example: The new crop grows well in moist soil.
items.note: The upper layer of earth in which plants ordinarily grow.

items.example: She recorded the demonstration with her smartphone.
items.note: A mobile phone with computing functions and applications.

items.example: The inspector entered the readings on a tablet.
items.note: A portable touch-screen computer; also studied in Unit 34.

items.example: They watched the documentary on a 3D TV using special glasses.
items.note: A television designed to display images with an impression of depth; a book-era consumer technology.

items.pt: câmera de vídeo de alta definição
items.example: They used a high-definition camcorder to film the prototype.
items.note: A dedicated video camera that captures detailed footage; HD means high-definition.

items.example: The satnav guided us around the roadworks.
items.note: British English abbreviation for satellite navigation; not the same as the GPS positioning system itself.

items.example: The vehicle uses GPS to estimate its location.
items.note: Global Positioning System; satellite-based location technology.

items.example: The digital photo frame changes pictures every minute.
items.note: A display designed to show photographs electronically.

items.example: The laboratory will experiment with a different type of sensor.
items.note: Experiment with something means test it to discover how it behaves.

items.example: The algorithm can utilise data from several sensors.
items.note: Formal or technical alternative to use; British spelling utilise.

items.example: Press a button to begin the calibration routine.
items.note: Use press, rather than push, in many descriptions of buttons.

items.example: The warning light began to flash during the test.
items.note: Of a light, switch on and off repeatedly or shine briefly.

items.example: The operator had to pull a lever to release the clamp.
items.note: A natural verb–noun combination for mechanical controls.

items.example: This lever controls the flow of liquid through the valve.
items.note: A rigid handle or bar that transmits force or controls a mechanism.

items.example: The shaft began to rotate at a constant speed.
items.note: A relatively formal or technical verb for turn around an axis.

items.example: Students dissected the specimen to examine its internal organs.
items.note: Cut open an organism or specimen to study its parts.

items.example: The chemist extracted a substance from the solution.
items.note: A formal or technical verb meaning take something out of something else.

items.example: The imaging system creates a model of the organ.
items.note: A body part with a particular biological function.

items.example: The scientists combined the two materials in a sealed container.
items.note: Join things together; pattern: combine A with B.

items.example: The label identifies the chemical used in the experiment.
items.note: A substance with a distinct chemical composition; also an adjective.

items.example: The solution may react with the metal at high temperatures.
items.note: In chemistry, substances react with one another.

items.example: The chemicals reacted violently, so the test was stopped.
items.note: Here the adverb describes the intensity of a chemical reaction.

items.example: The engineers will analyse the data before modifying the design.
items.note: British spelling analyse; American analyze.

items.example: The researchers concluded that the first model was unreliable.
items.note: Pattern: conclude that + clause, after considering evidence.

items.example: A serious flaw in the design caused repeated failures.
items.note: An imperfection or weakness; often a flaw in a theory, plan or design.

items.example: Their results did not support the original theory.
items.note: In science, an explanatory framework supported and tested using evidence.

items.example: Insert the card into the reader before starting the test.
items.note: Formal or technical alternative to put in; usually insert something into something.

items.example: Please install the driver before connecting the board.
items.note: Make software or equipment ready for use.

items.example: You can download the updated software from the project website.
items.note: Transfer data from a remote system to a local device.

items.pt: unidade de DVD; leitor ou gravador de DVD
items.example: The old computer has a DVD drive for optical discs.
items.note: A drive used to read or sometimes write DVDs; a technology shown in the textbook.

items.example: The scientists compared hereditary features in related plants.
items.note: Features passed between generations through genetic information.

items.example: The research focuses on ways to manipulate DNA in laboratory conditions.
items.note: An exercise phrase meaning deliberately alter or work on genetic material.

units.title: Unit 34 — Computers
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 34. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Computers, hardware, software and digital operations
learningObjectives: Distinguish computer hardware, software, devices, data storage and temporary memory.
Describe common applications, user-interface elements and networked systems.
Use standard computer verbs and phrasal verbs for entering, saving, backing up, deleting and upgrading data or software.
Recognise interface collocations and practical action patterns used in computing exercises.

sectionsChecked: A: Hardware definitions, storage, memory, microchips and networks
B: Software categories, applications, on-screen components and graphic interface vocabulary
C: Backups, deletion, system failures, keyboard input, upgrades and executing software
Exercises 34.1–34.3, numbered figures and printed answer key, including formatting and double-clicking

items.example: The technician checked the hardware before reinstalling the program.
items.note: The physical equipment of a computer system, contrasted with software.

items.example: She uses a personal computer for most of her design work.
items.note: Often abbreviated to PC; a computer intended for individual use.

items.example: A desktop computer is available at each laboratory workstation.
items.note: Typically a non-portable personal computer used on a desk.

items.example: He carried his laptop to the engineering workshop.
items.note: Portable personal computer with an integrated screen and keyboard.

items.example: The technician filled in the checklist on a tablet.
items.note: Portable computer mainly controlled using a touch screen.

items.example: The touch screen allows visitors to select a language.
items.note: A display that also accepts input through touch.

items.example: She saved the original images on the hard disk.
items.note: A storage device for data; unlike RAM, it keeps data when power is removed.

items.pt: unidade de disco; leitor ou gravador de discos
items.example: The disk drive failed to read the old backup.
items.note: A device that reads data from a disk and may also write to it.

items.example: We used a scanner to digitise the signed document.
items.note: In this unit, a device for converting paper documents and pictures into digital files.

items.example: He copied the slides onto a memory stick before the meeting.
items.note: Common term for a portable flash-storage device, often connected by USB.

items.example: Plug the memory stick into an available USB port.
items.note: Insert a plug or device into a compatible socket.

items.example: This application needs more RAM to process the images quickly.
items.note: Random access memory: temporary working memory, not long-term file storage.

items.example: Random access memory is used while programs are running.
items.note: The full name of RAM; the data normally disappears when power is removed.

items.example: The file occupies almost one gigabyte of storage.
items.note: An information-capacity unit; abbreviated GB.

items.example: A microchip inside the controller processes the sensor signals.
items.note: An integrated circuit containing many very small electronic components.

items.example: Silicon is a semiconductor used in many chips.
items.note: A material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled.

items.example: The microchip contains a complex electronic circuit.
items.note: A connected arrangement of electronic components.

items.example: The computers exchange results over a local computer network.
items.note: A group of connected computers or other devices that communicate.

items.pt: conectado em rede; interligado por rede
items.example: All the office printers are networked.
items.note: Connected so that computers and devices can communicate or share resources.

items.example: The two departments share information through a secure database.
items.note: A common verb–noun pairing for exchanging digital information.

items.example: The new software helps engineers analyse measurements.
items.note: Uncountable in standard English: software, not softwares.

items.example: The application generates a report after each test.
items.note: Software designed for a particular user task, often shortened to app.

items.example: I installed an app to record my study sessions.
items.note: Informal shortening of application, especially common on mobile devices.

items.example: She used word-processing software to prepare the minutes.
items.note: Creating, editing and formatting text in a computer program.

items.example: The team used a spreadsheet to compare the test results.
items.note: A grid-based document or application for organising data and calculations.

items.example: The database holds the calibration records for each device.
items.note: An organised collection of electronically stored information.

items.example: The simulation uses computer graphics to show the moving parts.
items.note: Images created or displayed with the help of computer software.

items.example: An antivirus scan detected a computer virus in the downloaded file.
items.note: Malicious code that can spread through systems and damage or interfere with data or programs.

items.example: The display shows the current temperature and pressure.
items.note: As a noun here, the screen or the information shown on it.

items.example: A warning appeared on the screen during startup.
items.note: A device surface where electronic information is shown.

items.example: Select the folder icon to open the project files.
items.note: A small graphical symbol representing a function, file or app.

items.example: Move the cursor to the end of the sentence.
items.note: An on-screen position indicator, such as an arrow or text insertion mark.

items.example: Click on the settings icon to change the display language.
items.note: Standard computer-use pattern: click on a button, icon or link.

items.example: Open a program and load the data file.
items.note: Open describes starting or accessing software via an interface.

items.example: The device can store information for several months.
items.note: Store means keep data so it can be used later.

items.pt: fazer backup; criar cópia de segurança
items.example: Back up your files before you install the update.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb: back up a file or back a file up.

items.example: We restored the missing documents from a backup.
items.note: The noun is usually one word; the phrasal verb is back up.

items.example: The system backs up its data on a regular basis.
items.note: A more formal way of saying regularly.

items.example: Please delete the duplicate entry from the table.
items.note: Remove text, files or other digital items.

items.example: I accidentally deleted the final paragraph.
items.note: Adverb meaning not intentionally.

items.example: The computer may crash if it runs out of memory.
items.note: When software or a computer stops functioning unexpectedly.

items.example: Use Undo if you remove the wrong section of text.
items.note: Reverse a recent action in an application; past tense undid.

items.example: Key in your password before accessing the system.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb for entering information using a keyboard.

items.example: I saved the file in the wrong folder by mistake.
items.note: Describes an unintended action or error.

items.pt: atualizar; melhorar a versão ou capacidade
items.example: We plan to upgrade the laboratory computers next year.
items.note: Replace or improve hardware or software with a more capable version.

items.example: The old computer cannot run software that requires more memory.
items.note: Run describes executing a program, not moving physically.

items.example: You can download an upgrade from the manufacturer's website.
items.note: Download transfers an update from a remote source to your device.

items.example: The operating system manages memory and hardware resources.
items.note: Core system software that manages hardware and provides services to applications.

items.pt: potente; com grande capacidade de processamento
items.example: A more powerful computer processed the images in half the time.
items.note: When describing computers, means greater capability or processing performance.

items.example: We scanned the handwritten document to keep a digital copy.
items.note: Handwritten means written by hand rather than typed.

items.example: Use the toolbar to format text consistently across the document.
items.note: Change the appearance or layout of text.

items.pt: clicar duas vezes; dar clique duplo
items.example: Double-click the file to open it in the default application.
items.note: Quickly click twice on the same item; whether necessary depends on the interface.

items.example: We keep the customer database up to date after each change.
items.note: Common pattern: keep something up to date.

items.example: Select the relevant rows before generating the chart.
items.note: Choose or highlight an item or part of a document.
